title: Docker Compose
summary: Running a whole app (PostgreSQL, a Django API and a React front end) as one system with Docker Compose: services, networks and volumes, Gunicorn as Django's production server, Nginx serving the React build and passing /api requests to Django, and running migrations inside containers. Step-by-step guide arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Run a database, a Django API and a React front end together from one docker-compose.yml, with Nginx in front.

steps.title: Do Docker's Compose quickstart
steps.detail: The official quickstart builds a tiny two-service app. It shows the `docker compose` commands you'll use every day.
steps.code:
docker compose version
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose down
steps.doneWhen: `docker compose ps` lists the quickstart's services as running.

steps.title: Read the curriculum's project layout
steps.detail: The Full-Stack module expects `client/` (React + Vite), `server/` (Django) and `db/` folders, each with its own Dockerfile. Your Netflix app (assignments/week-02/netflix) is still a flat layout, so compare it to this one.
steps.doneWhen: You can say which folder each part of a full-stack app goes in.

steps.title: Learn how containers find each other
steps.detail: Read the Compose networking page. Inside Compose, each service is reachable by its service name.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain why Django connects to host `db` instead of `localhost` inside Compose.

concepts.meaning: One container definition in docker-compose.yml, like db, server or client.
Storage that outlives a container, so the database keeps its data.
A private network Compose creates so services can reach each other by name.
A production server that runs Django; it replaces `runserver`.
A web server that serves the React files and forwards /api requests to Django.
